This paper proposes a model-based planning and RL framework that directly optimizes action durations, enabling temporally extended actions that improve planning efficiency and reduce compounding model errors. The method is simple, novel, and broadly applicable. Reviewers pointed out the limited evaluation on simple environments, leaving questions about scalability to complex, long-horizon problems, as well as the unclear explanation of search space reduction. In rebuttal, the authors clarified their formulation but did not add new experiments. 

Overall, I recommend acceptance: the conceptual contribution is strong, the results are promising, and the approach has high potential impact despite the limited empirical validation.

Thank you for taking the time to review our work and all of your thoughtful comments. Please find our responses to the questions below:

- For the questions regarding update-to-data ratio and the training of $F_{TE}$, we begin by providing the pseudocode for the entire data collection and training loop (for fixed $\delta t_{\max}$}) explicitly . In the algorithm,  $n$ refers to the number of training iterations, $D$ is the dataset and $b$ is the batch size.
  
  ``` 
  for i = 1 to n
    // Data collection
    for t = 1 to end of episode
        a_t = planner.choose_action(s_t)
        s_{t+1}, r_{t} = env.step(a_t)
        D = D.append((s_t, a_t, r_t, s_{t+1}))
    // Training
    num_of_batches = len(D)/b
    for j = 1 to num_of_batches
        sample a mini-batch of size b from D
        compute the loss and the gradients due to the mini-batch
        update the dynamics model using the gradient
  ```

  Note here that to be in sync with the notation in the main paper, $a_t$ includes the duration as well. More explicitly, $a_t$ is simply a concatenation of $|\mathcal{A}|$ primitive action variables and one variable for the action duration. 

  So, the number of updates depends on the size of the dataset. 

  Regarding the training of $F_{TE}$, as implicit in the pseudo-code, the $(s_t,a_t,r_t,s_{t+1})$ in the dataset are exactly the ones selected by the planner, i.e., the model is trained on the temporally-extended actions that were used in the episode. We do not add any implied transitions to the dataset. 

- To compare the prediction error between $F_{TE}$ and $F_{IP}$, we ran two experiments by randomly initializing action sequences (of length 500), and computing the MSE between the next state means predicted due to the two models and the states actually observed by taking the same actions in the environment. If an action resulted in termination, the environment was reset. For each environment, the models were taken from similar training iterations (indicated by $T_{ID}$ in the table) ensuring that the scores had stabilized
    
  The difference between the two experiments lies in the duration of the actions. Random one-step sequences (cols 4-5 in the table below) comprises of actions of duration $\delta t_{\min}$. For random temporally-extended sequences (cols 6-8 in the table below), action duration $\sim U(\delta t_{\min}, \delta t_{\max})$. For each environment, the values of $\delta t_{\min}$ and $\delta t_{\max}$ are the same as in the paper. Each experiment is repeated 10 times in order to get a better estimate and we report the means below:

  |                               |       |       | Random one step sequences |          | Random temporally extended sequences |          |                           |
  |-------------------------------|-------|-------|---------------------------|----------|--------------------------------------|----------|---------------------------|
  | Env                           | $\delta t_{\min}$ | $\delta t_{max}$ | $F_{TE}$                  | $F_{IP}$ | $F_{TE}$                             | $F_{IP}$ | $F_{IP}$ without outliers |
  | Cartpole $(T_{ID} = 200)$     |   1    |  10     |        0.0107                   |     $2.514 \times 10^{-7}$     |    0.0184                                  |    0.065      |                 0.065          |
  | Ant $(T_{ID} = 401)$          |     0.01  |  0.07     |            0.126               |  0.0149        |           0.298                          |   $4.525 \times 10^{10}$        |    0.60                      |
  | Half Cheetah $(T_{ID} = 301)$ |     0.01  |  0.07     |                0.30           |     0.04     |             1.752                         |    2.526      |    2.526                       |

  When using random temporally-extended action sequences, in 4 out of 10 experiments the MSE due to $F_{IP}$ explodes. We hypothesize that the states observed during these experiments probably were outside the range of examples seen during the training of the single-step model used by $F_{IP}$. In $F_{IP}$ without outliers, we report the MSE after removing such experiments.

  As can be observed, for one-step sequences, $F_{IP}$ has a lower MSE, but when we evaluate on temporally-extended action sequences, the models incur a higher MSE. This is expected as we make a lot more forward passes through the model when using $F_{IP}$ and hence the error starts to accumulate. 

- The comparison between a fixed $\delta t$ and our proposed approach might depend on the domain being considered. For example, consider the Dubins car environment. For a simple map that requires the car to go in a straight line, a large fixed $\delta t$ would work extremely well, but if we introduce obstacles, one would require a small value of $\delta t$. A map that has both of these elements (portions where the car has to travel straight for a long while, and portions where it has to navigate obstacles) would require one to have a conservative value of $\delta t$. In such situations, having a dynamic approach can be very helpful as the agent is free to adjust the action duration depending on its current position.

  Having said that, having a fixed $\delta t$ does reduce the computation load on the system. There are environments like Half Cheetah, where for the majority of the episode, the agent takes steps of approximately the same duration even while using the proposed dynamic approach. In such situations, it might be better to just use a fixed value of $\delta t$. 

  Figure 4 in the paper does touch upon this a bit. For Ant and Half Cheetah, we see that the histogram shows that most of the times, the agent takes an action with similar $\delta t$, however in Hopper the distribution is quite spread out. 

Thank you again for all your valuable feedback and we hope that we were able to clarify all the questions.

Thank you for taking the time to review our work and all your thoughtful comments. Please find our responses to the questions below:

-  When comparing the MAB to a fixed $\delta t_{\max}$ we are comparing to a good (manually tuned) value of $\delta t_{\max}$. Hence it is natural for the search for a value of $\delta t_{\max}$ to converge slower. What the experiments show is that the algorithm is able to self-tune $\delta t_{\max}$ through the MAB framework and achieve the same quality results. 

- We do lose granularity when using $A_{TE}$ and this can be detrimental in problems where longer actions cannot be used. In such cases $A_{TE}$ with a longer search horizon will have similar complexity for $A_{STD}$ (except for increasing the actions space by one dimension) and should perform similarly. In some cases, however, very deep search horizon is too expensive computationally.

- While our experiments with MuJoCo do have shorter horizons, our experiment with u-map in Dubins Car has a planning horizon of 75 (line 256). We did experiment with longer planning horizons for Dubins Car, but since the agent was able to reach with a shorter horizon, we chose the smaller value. We do acknowledge that in this experiment, we use an exact transition function rather than a learned model. 
    
  However, we think that in any case (learned or exact model), for many practical purposes, using primitive actions for planning result in a larger planning horizon than our proposed framework, and from past work [1] we know that longer planning horizons do lead to compounding errors. So we expect our proposed framework to perform better as compared to planning with primitive actions.

- The comparison to MFRL is interesting. We do not have a direct comparison, but thanks to [2], we know that PETS has much better sample complexity than some of the MFRL algorithms, and the baseline algorithm we use, $A_{STD}$, is essentially the PETS agent. So, we think we can safely assume that the sample complexity of our method would be much better than the MFRL algorithms presented in [2]. 

- We think the question was meant for Figure 3 since Figure 2 is for experiments with u-map. 

  First, we provide the pseudocode for the data collection and training loop for a fixed $\delta t_{\max}$ as it might help clarify things better. In the algorithm,  $n$ refers to the number of training iterations, $D$ is the dataset and $b$ is the batch size.

  ``` 
  for i = 1 to n
    // Data collection
    for t = 1 to end of episode
        a_t = planner.choose_action(s_t)
        s_{t+1}, r_{t} = env.step(a_t)
        D = D.append((s_t, a_t, r_t, s_{t+1}))
    // Training
    num_of_batches = len(D)/b
    for j = 1 to num_of_batches
        sample a mini-batch of size b from D
        compute the loss and the gradients due to the mini-batch
        update the dynamics model using the gradient
  ```
Note here that to be in sync with the notation in the main paper, $a_t$ includes the duration as well. 

  In Figure 3, we plot the agent's performance against the training iterations. As described in the pseudocode above, one training iteration corresponds to one episode worth of data collection. For MuJoCo, the duration of one episode (by which we mean the number of primitive steps taken during one episode) is fixed, while for Cartpole, the max duration per episode is fixed but the actual duration depends on if and when the pole falls.

Thank you again for all the valuable feedback and we hope that we were able to clarify all the questions.

Thank you for taking the time to review our work, for catching the typos and all your thoughtful comments. Please find our responses to the questions below:

- Our model has only a single action duration for all the action variables. So, at present, it does support action concurrency (when different action variables correspond to different parallel actions) but with the constraint that all action variables need to have the same duration. The extension to include multiple action durations would be an interesting (but challenging) extension.

-  Our model is not an exact continuous time model but does not work in discrete unit length steps. Referring to lines 134-136 and Algorithm A1 (line 479 in the appendix): We assume access to a model that can simulate correctly all steps with duration up to $\delta_t^{\text{env}}$ and allow the planner to choose duration of arbitrary real values where $F_{IP}$ will perform a "fractional action" in its last iteration. As we say in line 136 this is not an exact integration of the reward. 

- Similar to the previous question, we do not have access to a continuous time model but instead assume a simulator with a correct simulation for up to $\delta_t^{env}$. The effects evolve sequentially in that model, i.e., not in a sum but with a repeated sequential function application. 

Thank you again for all the valuable feedback and we hope that we were able to clarify all the questions.

Thank you for taking the time to review our work, for catching the hyperlink issue and all your thoughtful comments. Please find our responses to the questions below:

- We are indeed performing model-based planning as pointed out. However, we think MBRL is an umbrella term that includes model-based planning and this terminology has been used in the literature in the past. For example, [1] and [2]. [3] benchmarks MBRL algorithms and includes solutions which do not need to learn a policy.

- In Algorithm 1, we do not specify the details of the update as the algorithm is written for any shooting based planner. For our experiments, we use CEM. In order to update its action distribution, it looks at the top-k rewarding action sequences (after the for loop in lines 3-8), and then the mean and standard deviation of the action distribution is set to be the mean and standard deviation of the top-k action sequences.
    
- $f: S \times \mathcal{A} \rightarrow \Delta S$, $F = S \times (\mathcal{A} \cup \delta t) \rightarrow \Delta S$. The ranges and domains of $F_{IP}$ and $\hat{F}_{TE}$ are the same as $F$.

- We thank you for bringing the hyperlink issue to our notice. We had to move the explicit definition of $F_{IP}$ to the Appendix (Section A) due to lack of space, but it is defined concisely in the main text in lines 149-151.

    We wanted the arms to be exponentially spaced rather than linear, and hence we set $m = \log_2(T)$ where $T = \text{max primitive steps}$. Here max primitive steps is set by the environment. For simplicity, assuming the environment timescale is 1, the set of arms are $\{ T/2, T/4, T/8, \dots, T/2^m \}$.

    Equation 3 is a UCB-like metric where we use exponential-moving average of the reward rather than simply the average reward. This is done as the underlying dynamics model is changing and the older rewards might not reflect the current model.

- We do not fully understand the source of the equation being proposed, but we think the claim that we make is true. Firstly, to clarify, the claim made is for $A_{TE}$ with a fixed $\delta t_{\max}$ and does not include the MAB framework. (In the paper, we overload the term $A_{TE}$ to include the bandit framework, but the bandit framework is like a hyperparameter search, and each bandit technically corresponds to a single $A_{TE}$ agent.)
    
    Secondly, we add just a single action duration variable to the action space regardless of the number of action variables. So, the size of action space for $A_{STD}$ = $|\mathcal{A}|$ while the size of action space for $A_{TE} = |\mathcal{A}| + 1$. 

    For simplicity, let the environment timescale be 1 and let us consider $A_{STD}$ first. It has a fixed planning horizon $H$. So the computation graph that is created will have $H|\mathcal{A}|$ variables.

    Now let us consider $A_{TE}$ with a planning horizon of $H_1$ with a fixed $\delta t_{\max} = m$ (This is same as line 185 with $\delta_t^{\text{env}} = 1$). So the computation graph in this case will have $H_1(|\mathcal{A}|+1)$ variables. $A_{TE}$ will select actions with duration in the range $(1, m)$. For most practical purposes, the action duration will be greater than 1. This means we can set $H_1$ to be less than $H$ in order to have a similar effect.  

    Comparing $H_1$ and $H$ exactly is not possible without the actual action duration values. But let us assume that the $A_{TE}$ always chooses a fixed action duration $m_1 \in (1, m)$. Then $A_{TE}$ with $H_1 = H/m_1$ should have a similar reach as $A_{STD}$ that has a planning horizon of $H$. 
    
    We hope this clears out any confusion that might have been present regarding our claim.

- In all the experiments that we perform, the same configuration (number of neural networks in the ensemble, number of samples, number of planning iterations, batch-size, learning rate etc) is used for $A_{STD}$ and $A_{TE}$. In the paper, we mention that both the agents use the same architecture (line 217), but we should have added that they use the same configuration as well. 
    
    For $A_{STD}$ and $A_{TE}$, we learn an ensemble of 5 neural networks. For the bandit framework with $A_{TE}$, we learn an ensemble (of 5 neural networks) for each bandit arm. Before beginning an iteration (which comprises of one episode of data collection followed by learning), we select one bandit arm, and hence only one ensemble of neural networks is active.

Thank you again for all the valuable feedback and we hope that we were able to clarify all the questions. 

References:


[1] Deep reinforcement learning in a handful of trials using probabilistic dynamics models (Chua et al.)


[2] Integrating Sample-Based Planning and Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (Walsh et al.)


[3] Benchmarking model-based reinforcement learning (Wang et al.)

summary.value: The paper introduces a novel approach for planning (and model-based reinforcement learning) that treats action duration as a decision variable. Instead of only issuing a primitive action at every simulator time-step, the agent samples both an action and how long to repeat it. To support this, the authors learn a temporally-extended dynamics model that predicts state-reward transitions over variable time gaps. They then frame the choice of the maximum admissible duration as a multi-armed bandit, where each arm corresponds to an upper-bound $\delta t_{max}$. The resulting “action-plus-duration” space is then embedded inside a cross-entropy method (CEM) planner from prior works. Experiments on several continuous-control benchmarks (classic control, MuJoCo, Dubins car, Mountain Car) compare this temporally-extended agent ($A_{TE}$) against a baseline that plans with single-step actions ($A_{STD}$). $A_{TE}$ often reaches similar or higher episodic returns while requiring far fewer decision points and achieving notable wall-clock speed-ups. Impressively, $A_{TE}$ is also able to solve tasks which are unfeasible for $A_{STD}$ given compute and memory constraints.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
# Strengths

### Quality
- The motivation is sound with a clear goal. The authors provide simple neat method to address the practical burden of long horizons by letting the planner adjust its temporal resolution online.
- The paper delivers an end-to-end pipeline (bandit + ensemble world-model + CEM planner) and evaluates it in both pure-planning and learned-model settings.
- Across many domains $A_{TE}$ achieves equal-or-better return with fewer decisions and significantly faster training. The authors also provide an impressive number of hypermeter ablations. The ones on the effect of the different scale discount factors was particularly interesting.

### Clarity
- The high-level intuition (trading planning depth for breadth via action durations) is easy to follow, and the algorithmic components are standard.
- Visualisations of decision frequency and horizon length make the speed-up tangible.

### Significance
- A generic, task-agnostic way to obtain temporal abstractions could benefit robotics and MBRL practitioners.
- The work reconnects classical durative-action planning ideas with modern learned models.

### Originality
- Optimising action duration inside a sampling-based planner and adapting the duration range via a bandit scheme appears novel.
- Sparks theoretical questions about search-space complexity under temporal abstraction.

# Weaknesses

- The paper repeatedly frames itself as “MBRL” even though no policy is learned. Policy learning is a key key component of RL (see MBRL works like Dreamer for example). This work is closer to model-based planning with a learned simulator. This distinction needs to be explicit from the outset.

- There's a general lack of preciseness. For example, heavy reuse of “=” for definitions and equalities (esp. Sec. 3) hurts readability; “:=” or “≜” is recommended. It is also unclear how the update in step 9 of Algorithm 1 is done (Algorithm A1 references also hyperlinks to Algorithm 1). Section 4 is imprecise in general. 
  - Primitive dynamics function (f) and temporally-extended dynamics function (F) are not precisely defined. What are their domains and ranges?  
  - The iterative primitive dynamics function ($F_{IP}$) in line 151 is not defined nor explained in the main text despite being referred to throughout. 
  - It is unclear what the statement $\hat F_{TE} \approx F$ means. Does that sentence (line 159-160) mean the authors only use near-perfect models in the experiments? 
  - It is still unclear how the neural network is trained precisely. What is the input space, and what is the output space? What is the set of arms (is it $\\{\delta t_{min}, 2\delta t_{min}, ..., m\delta t_{min}\\}$)? What is "candidate i" in line 180 (is it a bandit arm i)? What's the informal justification for equation 3?
  - It seems like the approach also requires a suitable choice for m (for the number of arms and the upper-bound action duration arm), but this is not discussed.

- The claim "Using temporally-extended actions helps to reduce the space of possible trajectories" is false (line 192). It strictly increases the search space, since the search space now also includes the selection of action durations (and this is not even including the selection of $\delta t_{max}$). For $A_{TE}$, the search space is at least $\bigcup\limits_{k=1}^{m} (k|\mathcal{A}|)^{H/k}$. Similarly, the claim "$A_{TE}$ needs to optimize less variables than $A_{STD}$" is false (line 197).

- Hence one would expect $A_{TE}$ to take longer to plan due to the increase in the search space, but lead to shorter plans than $A_{STD}$ due to the temporally extended actions. However, this is not what is observed in the experiments. In fact, even when the authors demonstrate results in environments where temporally extended actions are not appropriate (Pusher and Reacher in Fig 3), $A_{TE}$ still performs similarly to $A_{STD}$ despite the much larger search space (and the fact that the dynamics model that is being learned is also more complex for $A_{TE}$). This suggests a potentially serious hyperparameter bias. That's $A_{TE}$ planning may be getting enough sequence samples, planning iterations, and model training batch-size to account for the increase in the search space size. Can the authors run ablations of these hyperparameters for $A_{TE}$?

- The approach uses several models in it's ensemble (for example a separate model for each bandit arm). It is unclear if the authors used the same total number of models for the baselines. Additionally, the use of only 5 seeds hurts the significance of the demonstrated results.

summary.value: This paper proposes a novel planning framework that dynamically adjusts the length of action repeats. The method automatically selects the optimal maximum repeat length with Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) problem. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating dynamic action repetition into planning-based methods significantly reduces the number of decision points, thereby accelerating planning, while also achieving better performance compared to no action repetition baselines. MAB-based selection of maximal action repeat range also performs reasonably well in practice.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strength**

**S1. Simplicity**
* The proposed method is conceptually straightforward and easy to implement.

**S2. Reduced Hyperparameter Tuning**
* An important hyperparameter, the maximum action duration ($\delta t_{\text{max}}$), is automatically tuned through the MAB-based approach, reducing the need for manual tuning.
* Moreover, the performance is robust to other parameters, such as discount factors (they indeed have a sweet-spot, but they do not have significant degradation on the overall performance ).

**S3. Thorough Analysis**
* The paper includes an in-depth analysis of various aspects of the proposed method, such as the effect of planning horizon, discount factor, and the use of model ensembles.

 

**Weaknesses**

**W1. Scalability to Complex Tasks**
* While the proposed method shows promise, its scalability to more complex tasks remains uncertain (experimental results are given for simple tasks). 
* Specifically, in planning, two main sources of error—model prediction error and optimization error—can accumulate over long horizons. 
* The paper does not fully address how these challenges are mitigated in high-dimensional or long-horizon tasks.

questions.value:
**Q1. Training Iteration vs. Number of Steps**
* What is the update-to-data (UTD) ratio used during training?

**Q2. Training of $F_{\text{TE}}$**
* How is the transition estimator ($F_{\text{TE}}$) trained? 
* Training such a model requires data that includes action durations. How is this data collected, and what supervision signal is used for training $F_{\text{TE}}$?

**Q3. $F_{\text{TE}}$ vs. $F_{\text{IP}}$**
* Can the authors provide a comparison of the prediction error between $F_{\text{TE}}$ (transition estimator with duration) and $F_{\text{IP}}$ (instantaneous predictor)? 
* This would help clarify the impact of modeling action durations for model prediction accuracies.

**Q4. Comparison with Fixed $\delta t$**
* In many cases, a fixed action repetition value is used (as also mentioned in the introduction). 
* How does the proposed dynamic approach compare quantitatively against models using a well-tuned fixed $\delta t$? Is dynamic repetition consistently better, or are there trade-offs?

final_justification.value:
The response have addressed the questions I had:
* The pseudocode effectively addressed most of the confusion I had regarding the training details.
* New experimental result clearly shows that $F_{TE}$ works better in long horizon rollouts than $F_{IP}$.
* The Dubins car example and the $\delta t$ distribution of hopper being spread out shows the importance of having variable $\delta t$.

Overall, I think this paper shows the potential and importance of using "variable length" of rollouts in planning.

summary.value:
The paper studies the challenge of modeling continuous time systems using discrete time dynamics, which often requires small simulation steps and large planning horizons. This can lead to computationally demanding planning problems and reduced performance. The authors propose an approach that involves controlling the continuous decision timescale directly by using temporally-extended actions. This allows the planner to treat the duration of the action as an additional optimization variable, alongside standard action variables.

The authors applied the approach to both planning and model-based RL. in the MBRL setting, the authors learn a dynamic model that is conditioned on the action and its duration. 
the author also propose to select the range of action duration dynamically over training using a multi-arm bandit method.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strength:
- the paper is well motivated and the approach is well presented. overall, it is easy to read the paper.
- the authors provide various experimental results and that illustrate the effectiveness of their approach in various environments, including both planning and MBRL.

Weakness: 
- MAB solution doesn't seem to improve over the simple fixed range. it converges much slower.
- planning over temporally extended action can indeed reduce the number of search space but we can lose control granularity. the author focus primarily on successful experiments, it would be helpful to discuss some failure cases.
- the experimental section focuses mainly on short-horizon tasks (locomotion continuous control tasks). do the authors expect that their method would work in really long-horizon task: for example navigation in big mazes.
- The authors compare only to planning with primitive actions. could the authors includes results with model-free RL? especially I am interested in there is any gain of the proposed method in term of sample complexity.
- Moreover, the sample complexity dimension is not discussed. I am not sure in in figure 2 the training iteration means environment interaction or gradient updates ?

value: NO or VERY MINOR ethics concerns only

final_justification.value:
The authors addressed most of my concerns.
But I still think that the paper don't provide convincing evidence of scalability of their approach to longer-horizon tasks with Learned Model.

Therefore, I maintain my score "borderline accept"

summary.value: The paper addresses the challenge of learning temporally extended actions in an MDP setting, for both planning and reinforcement learning. The proposed approach involves learning a transition model and reward estimates corresponding to repeating the same action over multiple time steps. The duration of each decision is also learned from experience using a non-stationary multi-armed bandit model. This method reduces search time in decision-making tasks by decreasing the number of decisions needed to reach a goal. The approach is evaluated across several benchmark domains.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. The model-based representation of temporally extended actions is intuitive and well-motivated.
2. The use of a non-stationary multi-armed bandit to model time step selection is innovative.
3. The method is supported by a comprehensive empirical analysis.

Weaknesses:
1. The distinctions and similarities between the proposed model and other temporal frameworks (e.g., semi-MDPs, co-MDPs, PDDL2.1) should be articulated more clearly.
2. The approach does not support fully continuous-time modeling.

questions.value:
1. Does the model support concurrency, as in other frameworks (e.g., Mausam and Weld, 2008)? If not, could it be extended to handle concurrent actions?
2. The temporal setting is not entirely clear to me. If I understand correctly, the model does not operate in fully continuous time but instead allows durations that are natural multiples of a standard time step. This seems more like an aggregated discrete-time setting than a true temporal one—is that correct?
3. Assuming the previous point is accurate, does this design eliminate the need to integrate over stochastic effects? In other words, are the resulting stochastic outcomes simply the sum of effects over the individual execution steps?

title.value: Improving planning and MBRL with temporally-extended actions

abstract.value: Continuous time systems are often modeled using discrete time dynamics but this requires a small simulation step to maintain accuracy. In turn, this requires a large planning horizon which leads to computationally demanding planning problems and reduced performance. Previous work in model-free reinforcement learning has partially addressed this issue using action repeats where a policy is learned to determine a discrete action duration. Instead we propose to control the continuous decision timescale directly by using temporally-extended actions and letting the planner treat the duration of the action as an additional optimization variable along with the standard action variables. This additional structure has multiple advantages. It speeds up simulation time of trajectories and, importantly, it allows for deep horizon search in terms of primitive actions while using a shallow search depth in the planner. In addition, in the model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) setting, it reduces compounding errors from model learning and improves training time for models. We show that this idea is effective and that the range for action durations can be automatically selected using a multi-armed bandit formulation and integrated into the MBRL framework. An extensive experimental evaluation both in planning and in MBRL, shows that our approach yields faster planning, better solutions, and that it enables solutions to problems that are not solved in the standard formulation.
